en: Could you please open the window?
tamil: தயவு செய்து ஜன்னலை திறக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a person nearby in a hot room.
explain: Could you please ...? is a soft, polite way to ask for a small favour.
usage: Use it with a neighbour, colleague or stranger when you need a small help.
leelaQ: If a room is very hot, what do you ask the person near the window?
answer: Could you please open the window? It is very hot here.

en: Excuse me sir, may I step inside for a moment?
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும் சார், நான் ஒரு நிமிஷம் உள்ள வரலாமா?
context: Knocking at your principal's room door.
explain: May I ...? is a formal way of asking permission. 'Excuse me' opens it politely.
usage: Use it at an office or school room door before entering.
leelaQ: You reach the principal's room and the door is closed. What do you say?
answer: Excuse me sir, may I step inside for a moment? I need your signature.

en: Would you mind helping me with this form?
tamil: இந்த படிவத்தை நிரப்ப எனக்கு உதவ முடியுமா?
context: Asking a bank staff member for help.
explain: Would you mind ...? is very polite. It is followed by the -ing form.
usage: Use it with bank or office staff when you do not understand a form.
leelaQ: How do you ask the bank staff to help you with a form?
answer: Would you mind helping me with this form? I am confused.

en: Could you lend me your calculator for five minutes?
tamil: உங்க கால்குலேட்டரை அஞ்சு நிமிஷம் கொடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a classmate for a calculator.
explain: Could you lend me ...? is a polite way to ask to use something for a short time.
usage: Use it with classmates or colleagues for small things.
leelaQ: Your calculator stopped working in class. What do you ask your friend?
answer: Could you lend me your calculator for five minutes? Mine is not working.

en: Please wait here, I will call him now.
tamil: தயவு செய்து இங்க காத்திருங்க, நான் இப்ப அவரை கூப்பிடறேன்.
context: Asking a visitor to wait at reception.
explain: 'Please' makes the instruction polite. 'I will' gives a quick promise.
usage: Use it as a receptionist or shop staff when a visitor arrives.
leelaQ: A guest comes to your office. What do you tell them politely?
answer: Please wait here, I will call the manager now.

en: Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the bus stand?
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், பஸ் ஸ்டாண்டுக்கு வழி சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a stranger for directions.
explain: Start with 'Excuse me' to get attention, then ask politely with 'could you'.
usage: Use it on the street when you are lost.
leelaQ: You are lost near a market. How do you ask for the bus stand?
answer: Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the bus stand?

en: I am sorry, I cannot come to the party tonight.
tamil: மன்னிச்சுக்கோங்க, இன்னிக்கு ராத்திரி பார்ட்டிக்கு என்னால வர முடியாது.
context: Politely refusing a party invitation.
explain: 'I am sorry' softens the refusal. 'Cannot' shows you are not able.
usage: Use it with friends or colleagues when you want to say no kindly.
leelaQ: A friend invites you to a party but you are busy. What do you say?
answer: I am sorry, I cannot come to the party tonight.

en: Shall I help you cross the road, uncle?
tamil: நான் உங்களை ரோடு கடக்க உதவட்டுமா அங்கிள்?
context: Offering help to an elderly man at a busy road.
explain: Shall I ...? is a polite offer to do something for someone.
usage: Use it to offer help to elders on busy roads.
leelaQ: You see an old man waiting at a busy road. What do you offer?
answer: Shall I help you cross the road, uncle? The traffic is heavy.

en: Will you have some juice or a cold drink?
tamil: உங்களுக்கு ஜூஸ் இல்ல கூல்ட்ரிங்க்ஸ் வேணுமா?
context: Offering a drink to a guest on a hot day.
explain: Will you have ...? is a friendly way to offer food or drink to guests.
usage: Use it when guests visit your home on a hot day.
leelaQ: A guest arrives at your home in the summer. What do you offer?
answer: Will you have some juice or a cold drink? It is very hot today.

en: Could you speak a little slowly, please?
tamil: கொஞ்சம் மெதுவா பேச முடியுமா?
context: Asking a fast speaker to slow down.
explain: 'A little slowly' makes the request gentle and clear.
usage: Use it on phone calls or meetings when you cannot follow the speed.
leelaQ: Someone speaks too fast on the phone. What do you say?
answer: Could you speak a little slowly, please? I did not understand.

en: Can you send me the file by evening?
tamil: சாயங்காலத்துக்குள்ள அந்த ஃபைலை எனக்கு அனுப்ப முடியுமா?
context: Asking a colleague for a file.
explain: 'By evening' gives a time limit in a polite way.
usage: Use it at work when you need a document from a teammate.
leelaQ: You need a report from your teammate today. How do you ask?
answer: Can you send me the file by evening? I need it for the meeting.

en: I would be happy to help you with that.
tamil: அதுல நான் உங்களுக்கு சந்தோஷமா உதவறேன்.
context: Offering help to a new colleague.
explain: 'I would be happy to' is a warm and polite way to offer help.
usage: Use it at work or with customers to sound friendly.
leelaQ: A new colleague is struggling with a task. What can you say?
answer: I would be happy to help you with that.

en: Please don't mention it, it was no trouble.
tamil: தயவு செய்து அதைப் பத்தி சொல்லாதீங்க, எனக்கு எந்த சிரமமும் இல்ல.
context: Replying to someone who thanks you.
explain: This is a polite reply to 'thank you'. It tells the person the help was easy.
usage: Use it when someone thanks you for a favour.
leelaQ: Your neighbour thanks you for helping. What do you reply?
answer: Please don't mention it, it was no trouble.

en: Can I use your phone to make a quick call?
tamil: ஒரு சின்ன கால் பண்ண உங்க ஃபோனை பயன்படுத்தலாமா?
context: Asking a stranger to use their phone.
explain: 'Quick' tells the person it will not take long, so they feel comfortable.
usage: Use it when your battery is dead or you have no balance.
leelaQ: Your phone battery is dead. What do you ask a stranger?
answer: Can I use your phone to make a quick call? My battery is dead.

en: Would it be possible to leave early today?
tamil: இன்னிக்கு சீக்கிரம் கிளம்ப முடியுமா?
context: Asking a manager for early leave.
explain: 'Would it be possible to ...?' is a very polite way to ask for permission.
usage: Use it with a boss when you need to leave before time.
leelaQ: You have a family function. How do you ask your manager for early leave?
answer: Would it be possible to leave early today? I have a function.

en: Thank you, but I am not hungry now.
tamil: நன்றி, ஆனா இப்ப எனக்கு பசிக்கல.
context: Politely refusing food at a friend's house.
explain: 'Thank you, but ...' is a gentle way to say no.
usage: Use it when a host offers food and you do not want it.
leelaQ: Your friend's mother offers food but you just ate. What do you say?
answer: Thank you, but I am not hungry now.

en: Could you hold the door for me, please?
tamil: எனக்காக கதவை பிடிச்சுக்கோங்களேன்.
context: Asking a person ahead of you in the lift.
explain: 'Hold the door' means keep it open. 'For me' makes it personal and polite.
usage: Use it in lifts and offices when your hands are full.
leelaQ: Your hands are full of boxes at a door. What do you ask?
answer: Could you hold the door for me, please?

en: Let me help you with those boxes.
tamil: அந்த பெட்டிகளை தூக்க நான் உதவறேன்.
context: Offering help to a colleague carrying boxes.
explain: 'Let me ...' is a friendly offer to do something for another person.
usage: Use it with friends and colleagues when you see them struggling.
leelaQ: A colleague carries many boxes. What do you offer?
answer: Let me help you with those boxes.

en: Is it okay if I sit next to you?
tamil: உங்க பக்கத்துல நான் உக்காரலாமா?
context: Asking a stranger on a bus about a seat.
explain: 'Is it okay if I ...?' is a soft way to ask for permission.
usage: Use it in buses, trains and waiting halls.
leelaQ: You find an empty seat in a bus. What do you ask the passenger?
answer: Is it okay if I sit next to you? The bus is very crowded.

en: Please give me five more minutes.
tamil: தயவு செய்து எனக்கு இன்னும் அஞ்சு நிமிஷம் கொடுங்க.
context: Asking a friend waiting for you.
explain: 'Please' with an imperative sounds polite when asking for time.
usage: Use it when you are getting ready and others are waiting.
leelaQ: Your friend is waiting outside but you are not ready. What do you say?
answer: Please give me five more minutes. I am almost ready.

en: Sorry, I am busy right now, can we talk later?
tamil: மன்னிச்சுக்கோங்க, நான் இப்ப பிஸி, அப்புறம் பேசலாமா?
context: Politely postponing a talk.
explain: Say sorry first, give a reason, then offer a new time.
usage: Use it with colleagues or family when you cannot talk now.
leelaQ: A friend wants to chat but you are working. What do you say?
answer: Sorry, I am busy right now, can we talk later?

en: Can you repeat that once more, please?
tamil: அதை இன்னொரு தடவை சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking someone to repeat in a meeting.
explain: 'Once more' means one more time. 'Please' keeps it polite.
usage: Use it when you did not hear or understand something.
leelaQ: You did not hear the instruction. What do you ask?
answer: Can you repeat that once more, please? I missed it.

en: I'm afraid we don't have that size in stock.
tamil: அந்த சைஸ் எங்ககிட்ட ஸ்டாக்ல இல்லன்னு நினைக்கிறேன், மன்னிக்கணும்.
context: A shop assistant refusing politely.
explain: 'I'm afraid' is a polite way to give bad news.
usage: Use it as shop staff when you must say no to a customer.
leelaQ: A customer asks for a size you do not have. What do you say?
answer: I'm afraid we don't have that size in stock, sir.

en: Could you bring me some hot water, please?
tamil: எனக்கு கொஞ்சம் சுடு தண்ணி கொண்டு வர முடியுமா?
context: Asking hotel staff for hot water.
explain: 'Could you bring me ...?' is a polite way to ask staff for something.
usage: Use it in hotels, hospitals and restaurants.
leelaQ: You are sick in a hotel room. What do you ask the staff?
answer: Could you bring me some hot water, please? I have a bad throat.

en: Would you please switch off the fan?
tamil: ஃபேனை நிறுத்த முடியுமா?
context: Asking a roommate to turn off the fan.
explain: 'Switch off' is common in Indian English for turn off.
usage: Use it at home or in a hostel when the fan is bothering you.
leelaQ: It is cold at night and the fan is on. What do you ask your roommate?
answer: Would you please switch off the fan? I am feeling cold.

en: Please come in and have a seat.
tamil: தயவு செய்து உள்ளே வாங்க, உக்காருங்க.
context: Welcoming a guest at home.
explain: This is a warm invitation. 'Have a seat' is a polite way to say sit down.
usage: Use it when a guest or visitor arrives.
leelaQ: A relative visits your house. How do you welcome them?
answer: Please come in and have a seat.

en: I would rather stay at home today, if you don't mind.
tamil: உங்களுக்கு பிரச்சனை இல்லன்னா இன்னிக்கு நான் வீட்டுலயே இருக்கறேன்.
context: Politely declining an outing.
explain: 'I would rather' shows your preference. 'If you don't mind' keeps it soft.
usage: Use it with friends or family when you do not want to go out.
leelaQ: Friends plan a movie but you are tired. What do you say?
answer: I would rather stay at home today, if you don't mind.

en: Can you lend me some money till Friday?
tamil: வெள்ளிக்கிழமை வரைக்கும் கொஞ்சம் காசு கடன் தர முடியுமா?
context: Asking a close friend for money.
explain: 'Lend' is what the giver does, 'borrow' is what you do. 'Till Friday' gives a clear time.
usage: Use it only with close friends or family.
leelaQ: You need small money until salary day. What do you ask a friend?
answer: Can you lend me some money till Friday? I will return it.

en: May I ask you a small favour?
tamil: நான் உங்ககிட்ட ஒரு சின்ன உதவி கேக்கலாமா?
context: Starting a request with a neighbour.
explain: This sentence opens the conversation before the real request. It prepares the listener.
usage: Use it before asking something bigger from a neighbour or colleague.
leelaQ: Before asking your neighbour for help, what do you say first?
answer: May I ask you a small favour?

en: Could you give me a lift to the station?
tamil: ஸ்டேஷன் வரைக்கும் என்னை விட முடியுமா?
context: Asking a colleague with a bike or car.
explain: 'Give me a lift' means take me in your vehicle.
usage: Use it with colleagues or neighbours who are going the same way.
leelaQ: It is raining and you have no auto. What do you ask your colleague?
answer: Could you give me a lift to the station? It is raining.

en: I will be glad to join you for lunch.
tamil: மதிய சாப்பாட்டுக்கு உங்ககூட சேர்ந்துக்க சந்தோஷம்.
context: Accepting a lunch invitation.
explain: 'I will be glad to' is a polite and warm way to accept.
usage: Use it to accept invitations from colleagues or friends.
leelaQ: A colleague invites you for lunch. How do you accept?
answer: I will be glad to join you for lunch.

en: Please don't be angry, it was my mistake.
tamil: தயவு செய்து கோபப்படாதீங்க, அது என் தப்பு.
context: Apologising to a friend.
explain: This sentence says sorry and accepts blame. 'Don't be angry' is a soft request.
usage: Use it when you did something wrong and want to calm the person.
leelaQ: You forgot a friend's birthday. What do you say?
answer: Please don't be angry, it was my mistake.

en: Is it okay if I bring my friend along?
tamil: என் நண்பனையும் கூட்டிட்டு வரலாமா?
context: Asking a host about bringing a friend.
explain: 'Is it okay if ...?' is a casual way to ask for permission.
usage: Use it with a host before taking another person to an event.
leelaQ: You are invited to a dinner. How do you ask about a friend?
answer: Is it okay if I bring my friend along?

en: Kindly send your reply as soon as possible.
tamil: தயவுசெஞ்சு உங்க பதிலை சீக்கிரம் அனுப்புங்க.
context: Writing a formal email request.
explain: 'Kindly' is formal and common in Indian office English.
usage: Use it in formal emails to ask for a quick response.
leelaQ: How do you end an email asking for a fast answer?
answer: Kindly send your reply as soon as possible.

en: Shall I say that once more, slowly?
tamil: நான் அதை இன்னொரு தடவ மெதுவா சொல்லட்டுமா?
context: Offering to repeat for a student.
explain: 'Shall I ...?' offers help without forcing it.
usage: Use it as a teacher or senior when someone looks confused.
leelaQ: Your friend did not follow your instructions. What do you offer?
answer: Shall I say that once more, slowly? I spoke too fast.

en: Can I take a message for him?
tamil: நான் அவருக்கு ஏதாவது செய்தி எடுத்துக்கட்டுமா?
context: Answering a phone call for a colleague.
explain: 'Take a message' means write down what the caller wants to say.
usage: Use it when the person the caller wants is not available.
leelaQ: Someone calls for your absent boss. What do you offer?
answer: Can I take a message for him? I will tell him.

en: I'm sorry, but he is not available right now.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், அவர் இப்ப இல்ல.
context: Telling a caller politely.
explain: 'Not available' is a polite phrase for not here or busy.
usage: Use it at reception or on the phone for a colleague who is out.
leelaQ: A caller asks for someone who is out. What do you say?
answer: I'm sorry, but he is not available right now.

en: Could you turn the music down a little?
tamil: மியூசிக்கை கொஞ்சம் குறைக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a neighbour about loud music.
explain: 'Turn down' means reduce the volume. 'A little' keeps it kind.
usage: Use it with neighbours or family members when noise is a problem.
leelaQ: The neighbour plays loud music late at night. What do you ask?
answer: Could you turn the music down a little? I am studying.

en: Please take your seat, the class will start soon.
tamil: தயவு செய்து உங்க இடத்துல உக்காருங்க, வகுப்பு சீக்கிரம் தொடங்கும்.
context: A teacher asking students to sit.
explain: 'Take your seat' is a polite way to say sit down.
usage: Use it as a teacher or trainer before starting a session.
leelaQ: You are the teacher and students are standing. What do you say?
answer: Please take your seat, the class will start soon.

en: Do you want me to book the tickets?
tamil: நான் டிக்கெட் புக் பண்ணட்டுமா?
context: Offering to book tickets for family.
explain: 'Do you want me to ...?' is a simple offer in everyday talk.
usage: Use it with family or friends when you can do a task for them.
leelaQ: Your family plans a trip. What do you offer to do?
answer: Do you want me to book the tickets? I will do it now.

en: I would really appreciate your help with this.
tamil: இதுல உங்க உதவியை நான் ரொம்ப மதிப்பேன்.
context: Asking a senior for help.
explain: 'I would appreciate' is a formal and respectful way to ask for help.
usage: Use it with seniors or clients when you need real support.
leelaQ: You need your senior's help on a hard task. What do you say?
answer: I would really appreciate your help with this.

en: Sorry, you can't park your vehicle here.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், இங்க வண்டி நிறுத்த முடியாது.
context: A security guard refusing politely.
explain: 'Sorry' makes a rule sound softer. 'Can't' tells what is not allowed.
usage: Use it as a guard or staff member to stop someone politely.
leelaQ: A visitor parks in a no-parking area. What do you say as the guard?
answer: Sorry, you can't park your vehicle here, sir.

en: Could I speak to the manager, please?
tamil: நான் மேனேஜர்கிட்ட பேசலாமா?
context: Asking at a shop or hotel.
explain: 'Could I speak to ...?' is the polite way to ask for a person on the phone or in person.
usage: Use it when you have a complaint or need a decision.
leelaQ: Your order is wrong. Whom do you ask to speak to?
answer: Could I speak to the manager, please?

en: Please share the notes with me when you are free.
tamil: நீங்க ஃப்ரீயா இருக்கும்போது அந்த நோட்ஸை எனக்கு ஷேர் பண்ணுங்க.
context: Asking a classmate for notes.
explain: 'When you are free' gives the other person freedom, so it sounds kind.
usage: Use it with classmates or colleagues for non-urgent requests.
leelaQ: You missed a class. How do you ask a friend for notes?
answer: Please share the notes with me when you are free.

en: I can drop you at your place if you want.
tamil: நீங்க விரும்பினா உங்க வீட்டுல உங்களை விடறேன்.
context: Offering a ride home to a friend.
explain: 'If you want' makes the offer optional and friendly.
usage: Use it with friends or colleagues after a late meeting.
leelaQ: It is late and your friend has no ride. What do you offer?
answer: I can drop you at your place if you want.

en: Would you be able to attend the meeting tomorrow?
tamil: நாளைக்கு மீட்டிங்குக்கு உங்களால வர முடியுமா?
context: Asking a colleague to attend.
explain: 'Would you be able to ...?' is polite for asking about someone's availability.
usage: Use it at work to check availability before fixing a plan.
leelaQ: You want a teammate at tomorrow's meeting. What do you ask?
answer: Would you be able to attend the meeting tomorrow?

en: No, thank you, I have already eaten.
tamil: வேண்டாம், நன்றி, நான் ஏற்கனவே சாப்பிட்டுட்டேன்.
context: Refusing second serving politely.
explain: 'No, thank you' is a clear and polite refusal. 'Already' shows it is done.
usage: Use it at a feast or party when the host keeps offering food.
leelaQ: A host offers more rice but you are full. What do you say?
answer: No, thank you, I have already eaten enough.

en: Could you check my answer sheet once again?
tamil: என் விடைத்தாளை இன்னொரு தடவை பாக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a teacher to recheck marks.
explain: 'Once again' is polite when asking for a second look.
usage: Use it with a teacher or examiner when you feel a mistake was made.
leelaQ: You think your marks are wrong. What do you ask the teacher?
answer: Could you check my answer sheet once again, madam?

en: Do tell me if there is anything you need.
tamil: உங்களுக்கு ஏதாவது தேவைன்னா கண்டிப்பா சொல்லுங்க.
context: Offering help to a new neighbour.
explain: 'Do tell me' makes the offer warm and sincere.
usage: Use it with guests, new neighbours or hotel customers.
leelaQ: Your new neighbour is moving in. What do you tell them?
answer: Do tell me if there is anything you need. I live next door.

en: Is it all right if I call you after dinner?
tamil: நான் சாப்பாட்டுக்கு அப்புறம் கூப்பிடலாமா?
context: Asking permission to call later.
explain: 'Is it all right if ...?' is a gentle way to ask permission.
usage: Use it with elders or colleagues when you want to call at a better time.
leelaQ: You want to call your uncle later. How do you ask?
answer: Is it all right if I call you after dinner?

en: Could you please keep this between us?
tamil: இதை நமக்குள்ளயே வச்சுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a friend to keep a secret.
explain: 'Between us' means a secret. 'Please' keeps it respectful.
usage: Use it with a close friend or trusted colleague.
leelaQ: You tell a friend a private matter. What do you ask?
answer: Could you please keep this between us?

en: I'll take care of the bill, please don't worry.
tamil: நான் பில்லை பாத்துக்கறேன், கவலைப்படாதீங்க.
context: Offering to pay at a restaurant.
explain: 'I'll take care of' means I will handle it. It is a kind offer.
usage: Use it when you want to treat friends or guests.
leelaQ: The bill comes at the end of a lunch. What do you offer?
answer: I'll take care of the bill, please don't worry.

en: Would you mind not talking loudly in the library?
tamil: லைப்ரரில சத்தமா பேசாம இருக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a person to be quiet in a library.
explain: 'Would you mind not ...?' is a very polite way to stop someone.
usage: Use it in public places when someone's noise disturbs you.
leelaQ: A person talks loudly while you study. What do you politely ask?
answer: Would you mind not talking loudly in the library? I am studying.

en: May I have your attention, please?
tamil: தயவு செய்து எல்லாரும் கொஞ்சம் கவனிக்கறீங்களா?
context: Starting an announcement.
explain: This is a formal phrase used to get a group's attention.
usage: Use it as a host, teacher or speaker before announcing something.
leelaQ: You must make an announcement in a hall. How do you begin?
answer: May I have your attention, please?

en: Can you help me carry this table upstairs?
tamil: இந்த மேசையை மாடிக்கு தூக்கிட்டு போக உதவ முடியுமா?
context: Asking a neighbour for physical help.
explain: 'Help me carry' uses a base verb after 'help me'. It is a short and clear request.
usage: Use it with neighbours or friends when a task needs two people.
leelaQ: You must move heavy furniture. What do you ask a neighbour?
answer: Can you help me carry this table upstairs?

en: I'm sorry to bother you, but is this seat taken?
tamil: தொந்தரவுக்கு மன்னிக்கணும், இந்த இடம் காலியா?
context: Asking in a cinema hall or train.
explain: 'Sorry to bother you' opens the question politely.
usage: Use it with strangers in theatres, trains or buses.
leelaQ: You see a seat with a bag on it. What do you ask?
answer: I'm sorry to bother you, but is this seat taken?

en: Please don't touch that, it is very hot.
tamil: தயவு செய்து அதை தொடாதீங்க, ரொம்ப சூடு.
context: Warning a child in the kitchen.
explain: 'Don't' plus 'please' gives a safe and gentle warning.
usage: Use it at home to stop children or guests from getting hurt.
leelaQ: A child goes near the stove. What do you say?
answer: Please don't touch that, it is very hot.

en: Could you recommend a good doctor near here?
tamil: இங்க பக்கத்துல ஒரு நல்ல டாக்டரை சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a neighbour for advice.
explain: 'Recommend' means suggest something good.
usage: Use it with neighbours or colleagues when you are new in an area.
leelaQ: You have moved to a new area. What do you ask your neighbour?
answer: Could you recommend a good doctor near here?

en: Please sit down, uncle. You look tired.
tamil: தயவுசெஞ்சு உக்காருங்க அங்கிள். சோர்வா தெரியறீங்க.
context: Offering a seat to an elderly man.
explain: 'Please sit down' is a polite offer of a seat, followed by a caring reason.
usage: Use it with elders, pregnant women or tired visitors.
leelaQ: An old man stands in a bus. What do you tell him?
answer: Please sit down, uncle. You look tired, so take my seat.

en: Can we please start the meeting a little later?
tamil: மீட்டிங்கை கொஞ்சம் தாமதமா தொடங்கலாமா?
context: Asking a team to change a time.
explain: 'We' makes the request about the group. 'Please' keeps it kind.
usage: Use it at work when a delay will help the team.
leelaQ: Half the team is stuck in traffic. What do you suggest?
answer: Can we please start the meeting a little later?

en: I wish I could, but I have another plan.
tamil: எனக்கும் வரணும்னு ஆசை, ஆனா எனக்கு வேற ஒரு பிளான் இருக்கு.
context: Politely refusing an invitation.
explain: 'I wish I could' shows you want to but cannot. It keeps the friendship warm.
usage: Use it with friends when you must refuse but want to be kind.
leelaQ: A friend invites you but you have other plans. What do you say?
answer: I wish I could, but I have another plan.

en: Would you please sign here?
tamil: தயவு செய்து இங்க கையெழுத்து போடுங்க.
context: A courier boy asking for a signature.
explain: 'Sign here' shows where. 'Would you please' makes the order polite.
usage: Use it as delivery staff or office staff when papers need a signature.
leelaQ: A courier delivers a parcel. What do you ask the receiver?
answer: Would you please sign here?

en: Don't worry, I will explain everything slowly.
tamil: கவலைப்படாதீங்க, நான் எல்லாத்தையும் மெதுவா விளக்கறேன்.
context: Calming a nervous new student.
explain: 'Don't worry' calms the listener. 'I will' makes a promise.
usage: Use it as a teacher or senior to give confidence.
leelaQ: A new student feels afraid. What do you say to help?
answer: Don't worry, I will explain everything slowly.

en: Could you give me your phone number, please?
tamil: உங்க ஃபோன் நம்பரை கொடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a new acquaintance for contact.
explain: 'Give me your number' is direct, so 'could you' and 'please' make it polite.
usage: Use it when you meet someone and want to stay in touch.
leelaQ: You meet a useful contact at a function. What do you ask?
answer: Could you give me your phone number, please?

en: Please make yourself comfortable.
tamil: தயவு செய்து வசதியா இருங்க.
context: Welcoming a guest.
explain: This phrase tells guests to relax and feel at home.
usage: Use it when a guest arrives at your home or office.
leelaQ: A guest looks nervous in your home. What do you say?
answer: Please make yourself comfortable.

en: Can I pay by card, or do you take only cash?
tamil: நான் கார்டுல கொடுக்கலாமா, இல்ல கேஷ் மட்டும்தான் வாங்குவீங்களா?
context: Asking a shopkeeper about payment.
explain: This question gives two options. It is common when shopping.
usage: Use it in shops and restaurants when you are not sure about payment.
leelaQ: You have no cash in a small shop. What do you ask?
answer: Can I pay by card, or do you take only cash?

en: I am afraid I cannot agree with you on this.
tamil: நான் இதுல உங்ககூட ஒத்துக்க முடியாதுன்னு பயப்படறேன்.
context: Disagreeing politely in a meeting.
explain: 'I am afraid' softens a disagreement. It sounds respectful.
usage: Use it in meetings or discussions when you have a different opinion.
leelaQ: You disagree with a colleague's idea. How do you say it kindly?
answer: I am afraid I cannot agree with you on this.

en: Could you please wait outside for a few minutes?
tamil: தயவு செய்து வெளியில சில நிமிஷம் காத்திருக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a visitor to wait outside.
explain: 'A few minutes' tells the person it will be short.
usage: Use it as staff or a host when you are not ready for the visitor.
leelaQ: A visitor arrives while you are in a meeting. What do you say?
answer: Could you please wait outside for a few minutes?

en: Please excuse me for being late.
tamil: தாமதமா வந்ததுக்கு தயவு செய்து மன்னிச்சுக்கோங்க.
context: Apologising when you arrive late.
explain: 'Excuse me for' plus -ing is a polite way to say sorry.
usage: Use it at meetings or classes when you reach after the start.
leelaQ: You enter a class ten minutes late. What do you say?
answer: Please excuse me for being late, madam.

en: Can I get a receipt for this payment?
tamil: இந்த பணத்துக்கு ஒரு ரசீது கிடைக்குமா?
context: Asking a shop for a bill.
explain: 'Get a receipt' is a common and polite way to ask for proof of payment.
usage: Use it in shops, offices and hospitals after paying.
leelaQ: You paid fees at the office. What do you ask for?
answer: Can I get a receipt for this payment?

en: I'll be happy to wait if you are busy.
tamil: நீங்க பிஸியா இருந்தா நான் சந்தோஷமா காத்திருக்கறேன்.
context: Telling a busy shopkeeper you can wait.
explain: 'If you are busy' shows you respect the other person's time.
usage: Use it with shopkeepers, doctors or officers who are occupied.
leelaQ: A clerk is busy with another customer. What do you say?
answer: I'll be happy to wait if you are busy.

en: Would you like to try this sweet?
tamil: இந்த இனிப்பை சாப்பிட்டு பாக்கறீங்களா?
context: Offering sweets to a visitor.
explain: 'Would you like to try ...?' invites someone to taste something.
usage: Use it during festivals or when guests visit.
leelaQ: It is Diwali and a guest arrives. What do you offer?
answer: Would you like to try this sweet? My mother made it.

en: Please keep your voice down, the baby is sleeping.
tamil: தயவு செய்து சத்தம் போடாதீங்க, குழந்தை தூங்குது.
context: Asking family members to be quiet.
explain: 'Keep your voice down' means speak softly. The reason is added after a comma.
usage: Use it at home or in a hospital when someone is resting.
leelaQ: Your baby is sleeping and guests are loud. What do you say?
answer: Please keep your voice down, the baby is sleeping.

en: Could you help me find this address?
tamil: இந்த முகவரியை கண்டுபிடிக்க எனக்கு உதவ முடியுமா?
context: Asking a shopkeeper for directions.
explain: 'Help me find' uses a base verb after 'me'.
usage: Use it with shopkeepers or auto drivers in a new place.
leelaQ: You hold a written address and are lost. What do you ask?
answer: Could you help me find this address?

en: I don't think I can finish it today, sorry.
tamil: இன்னிக்கு என்னால இதை முடிக்க முடியும்னு தோணல, மன்னிக்கணும்.
context: Telling a boss about a delay.
explain: 'I don't think' is softer than 'I cannot'. 'Sorry' adds politeness.
usage: Use it with a manager when a task will not be ready on time.
leelaQ: The report will not be ready today. What do you tell your boss?
answer: I don't think I can finish it today, sorry.

en: May I use your restroom, please?
tamil: நான் உங்க கழிவறையை பயன்படுத்தலாமா?
context: Asking in a shop or office.
explain: 'May I ...?' is polite and formal. 'Restroom' is a polite word for toilet.
usage: Use it in a shop, office or friend's house when you need the toilet.
leelaQ: You are on a long trip and need a restroom. What do you ask?
answer: May I use your restroom, please?

en: Let me know when you are free, and we can meet.
tamil: நீங்க ஃப்ரீயா இருக்கும்போது சொல்லுங்க, நாம சந்திக்கலாம்.
context: Setting up a meeting politely.
explain: 'Let me know' gives control to the other person.
usage: Use it with busy colleagues or relatives when planning a meet.
leelaQ: A busy friend wants to meet you. What do you reply?
answer: Let me know when you are free, and we can meet.

en: Would you like me to carry that for you?
tamil: நான் அதை உங்களுக்காக தூக்கட்டுமா?
context: Offering help at a railway station.
explain: 'Would you like me to ...?' is a gentle offer.
usage: Use it with elders or travellers who are struggling with luggage.
leelaQ: You see an elderly man with a heavy suitcase. What do you ask?
answer: Would you like me to carry that for you?

en: Could we sit somewhere quieter to talk?
tamil: பேச கொஞ்சம் அமைதியான இடத்துல உக்காரலாமா?
context: Suggesting a quieter place.
explain: 'Could we ...?' is a polite suggestion that includes both people.
usage: Use it when a place is noisy and you want a private talk.
leelaQ: The cafe is very noisy. What do you suggest?
answer: Could we sit somewhere quieter to talk?

en: I'm sorry, but I cannot accept this offer.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், ஆனா இந்த வாய்ப்பை என்னால ஏத்துக்க முடியாது.
context: Refusing a job offer politely.
explain: 'I cannot accept' is formal. 'I'm sorry, but' softens bad news.
usage: Use it in formal talks like job offers or business deals.
leelaQ: You get a job offer you cannot take. What do you say?
answer: I'm sorry, but I cannot accept this offer. I have another plan.

en: Please be careful, the floor is wet.
tamil: தயவு செய்து பாத்து போங்க, தரை ஈரமா இருக்கு.
context: Warning a visitor.
explain: A short warning with 'please' sounds caring, not rude.
usage: Use it at home, shops or offices after cleaning.
leelaQ: Someone enters a freshly mopped floor. What do you say?
answer: Please be careful, the floor is wet.

en: Could you share your screen, please?
tamil: தயவு செய்து உங்க ஸ்கிரீனை ஷேர் பண்ண முடியுமா?
context: Asking in an online meeting.
explain: 'Share your screen' is common in online meetings.
usage: Use it in video calls when you want to see someone's work.
leelaQ: In an online class, you want to see the student's work. What do you ask?
answer: Could you share your screen, please?

en: Do you need any help with your homework?
tamil: உங்க வீட்டுப்பாடத்துல ஏதாவது உதவி வேணுமா?
context: A parent offering help to a child.
explain: 'Do you need any help with ...?' is a simple offer.
usage: Use it with children, juniors or friends who are studying.
leelaQ: Your younger brother is studying late. What do you ask?
answer: Do you need any help with your homework?

en: Would you please move your bike a little?
tamil: தயவு செய்து உங்க பைக்கை கொஞ்சம் நகத்த முடியுமா?
context: Asking a neighbour to move a bike.
explain: 'A little' makes the request light. 'Would you please' is very polite.
usage: Use it when a vehicle blocks your gate or path.
leelaQ: A bike blocks your gate. What do you ask your neighbour?
answer: Would you please move your bike a little?

en: Thank you so much, you are very kind.
tamil: ரொம்ப நன்றி, நீங்க ரொம்ப நல்லவங்க.
context: Thanking someone who helped.
explain: 'You are very kind' praises the person after they help. It sounds sincere.
usage: Use it after anyone helps you, from a stranger to a boss.
leelaQ: A stranger helps you with directions. What do you say?
answer: Thank you so much, you are very kind.

en: Can you wake me up at six tomorrow?
tamil: நாளைக்கு காலைல ஆறு மணிக்கு என்னை எழுப்ப முடியுமா?
context: Asking a family member.
explain: 'Wake me up' means make me get up from sleep.
usage: Use it with family or roommates when you must get up early.
leelaQ: You have an early train tomorrow. What do you ask your mother?
answer: Can you wake me up at six tomorrow?

en: I will not be able to attend the function, I'm sorry.
tamil: என்னால விழாவுக்கு வர முடியாது, மன்னிச்சுக்கோங்க.
context: Declining a function invitation.
explain: 'Will not be able to' is a polite, formal way to say no.
usage: Use it with relatives or officials who invite you to events.
leelaQ: A relative invites you to a wedding but you are out of town. What do you say?
answer: I will not be able to attend the function, I'm sorry.

en: Can I take your order now, sir?
tamil: நான் இப்ப உங்க ஆர்டரை எடுக்கலாமா சார்?
context: A waiter asking a customer.
explain: 'Take your order' is what waiters say. 'Sir' adds respect.
usage: Use it as waiting staff in a hotel or restaurant.
leelaQ: You are a waiter and the guests have the menu. What do you ask?
answer: Can I take your order now, sir?

en: Please accept my apologies for the delay.
tamil: தாமதத்துக்கு என் மன்னிப்பை ஏத்துக்கோங்க.
context: A formal apology in an email.
explain: 'Accept my apologies' is formal and used in writing.
usage: Use it in emails or letters to customers and seniors.
leelaQ: You replied late to a client. How do you apologise formally?
answer: Please accept my apologies for the delay.

en: Could you tell me what time the shop opens?
tamil: கடை எத்தனை மணிக்கு திறக்கும்னு சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a security guard.
explain: 'Could you tell me ...?' is followed by a normal statement order, not a question order.
usage: Use it with guards or neighbours when planning a visit.
leelaQ: The shop is closed when you arrive. What do you ask the guard?
answer: Could you tell me what time the shop opens?

en: Take a short break. You have worked a lot.
tamil: கொஞ்சம் ப்ரேக் எடுங்க. ரொம்ப வேலை செஞ்சிருக்கீங்க.
context: Suggesting rest to a colleague.
explain: A friendly imperative suggestion, followed by the reason.
usage: Use it with colleagues or family who look tired.
leelaQ: Your friend has studied for hours. What do you suggest?
answer: Take a short break for ten minutes. You have studied a lot.

en: Allow me to introduce my friend, Priya.
tamil: என் நண்பி பிரியாவை அறிமுகப்படுத்தறேன்.
context: Introducing a friend formally.
explain: 'Allow me to' is a formal way to begin an introduction.
usage: Use it at functions or offices when you introduce two people.
leelaQ: You want to introduce a friend to your boss. How do you begin?
answer: Allow me to introduce my friend, Priya.

en: Could I trouble you for a glass of water?
tamil: ஒரு கிளாஸ் தண்ணி கொடுத்து உங்களுக்கு சிரமம் தரலாமா?
context: Asking a host very politely.
explain: 'Could I trouble you for ...?' is very polite and a bit formal.
usage: Use it at someone's house, especially with elders.
leelaQ: You feel thirsty at an elder's home. How do you ask?
answer: Could I trouble you for a glass of water?

en: Hey, can you pass me the salt?
tamil: ஏய், அந்த உப்பை எடுத்து கொடுக்கறியா?
context: Asking a friend at the dining table.
explain: 'Hey' and 'can you' show an informal level, good with friends and family.
usage: Use it with friends and family during meals.
leelaQ: At lunch you need salt. What do you ask your brother?
answer: Hey, can you pass me the salt?

en: Sorry yaar, I can't make it today.
tamil: சாரி யார், இன்னிக்கு என்னால வர முடியாது.
context: Refusing a friend in a casual way.
explain: 'Yaar' is casual Indian English for friend. Use it only with friends.
usage: Use it with close friends when you cannot join a plan.
leelaQ: A close friend asks you to join a match, but you are busy. What do you say?
answer: Sorry yaar, I can't make it today.

en: Do you want me to switch on the light?
tamil: நான் லைட்டை போடட்டுமா?
context: Offering in a dark room.
explain: 'Switch on' means turn on. It is common in India.
usage: Use it at home or hostel when the room is dark.
leelaQ: A guest sits in a dark room. What do you offer?
answer: Do you want me to switch on the light?

en: Can you keep an eye on my bag for a minute?
tamil: ஒரு நிமிஷம் என் பையை பாத்துக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a stranger at a station.
explain: 'Keep an eye on' means watch something carefully.
usage: Use it at stations or cafes when you leave for a short time.
leelaQ: You need to buy a ticket and leave your bag. What do you ask?
answer: Can you keep an eye on my bag for a minute?

en: I would be grateful if you could reply soon.
tamil: நீங்க சீக்கிரம் பதில் சொன்னா நான் நன்றியுடன் இருப்பேன்.
context: Formal email to a client.
explain: 'I would be grateful if you could' is a very formal and polite request.
usage: Use it in formal emails to officers, clients or teachers.
leelaQ: How do you politely ask a client for a quick answer?
answer: I would be grateful if you could reply soon.

en: Please don't feel bad, it happens to everyone.
tamil: தயவு செய்து வருத்தப்படாதீங்க, எல்லாருக்கும் இது நடக்கும்.
context: Comforting a friend after a mistake.
explain: This sentence comforts someone after a small failure.
usage: Use it with friends or juniors who made a mistake.
leelaQ: Your friend failed a small test. What do you say?
answer: Please don't feel bad, it happens to everyone.

en: Could you please lower your voice a little?
tamil: தயவு செய்து உங்க குரலை கொஞ்சம் குறைக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a loud caller in a library.
explain: 'Lower your voice' is a polite way to say speak softly.
usage: Use it in libraries, offices or trains when someone is too loud.
leelaQ: A person talks loudly in a library. What do you ask?
answer: Could you please lower your voice a little?
